sections.heading: Referral programs: incentivized, but potentially less sticky
sections.content: Shapiro says referral programs often select for people who mainly want the reward; their invitees may want the two-sided reward rather than the app, then leave without inviting others. He says this lacks the same compounding, sticky, retentive nature as product-led acquisition. He is not categorically against them: “If you can make [them] work though, fantastic.”

sections.heading: Billboarding: exposure built into product use
sections.content: Billboarding is when using a product makes it visible to people around you—the product advertises itself. Examples include Hotmail or iPhone email signatures, and shareable Calendly links, Dropbox file links, or GoFundMe pages. Shapiro describes it as free exposure that can scale and compound, while noting it is especially promising when the product lends itself to this kind of visibility or sharing.

answer.summary: Shapiro is skeptical of incentivized referral programs because they can attract reward-seekers who may not stick around; billboarding instead makes ordinary product use advertise the product, offering free exposure that can scale and compound.

sections.heading: Referral programs
sections.content: He says referral programs often select for people who want the reward, and their invitees may want the two-sided reward rather than the product, then leave without inviting others. He sees this as lacking the sticky, compounding nature of product-led acquisition based on users naturally getting more value by inviting others, rather than needing an artificial incentive. He allows that referral programs can work, but is not generally a fan.

sections.heading: Billboarding
sections.content: Billboarding is when product use is inherently visible and the product advertises itself. Examples include Hotmail or iPhone email signatures and Calendly links users share to schedule events. Shapiro describes it as a free source of exposure that can scale infinitely and have compounding effects. The tradeoff, then, is between paying or relying on incentives that may bring in reward-driven users and building visibility into product use itself; billboarding’s benefits depend on the product naturally lending itself to visible sharing.
